stops.name: Las Tres Acequias, patriot blood by patriot hands
stops.campa: The quarrel of the two houses comes to powder: Carrera has retaken the government by coup, and on 26 August 1814, at the three irrigation channels south of the Maipo, O'Higgins's division and Carrera's fire on one another. Patriot kills patriot within earshot of the advancing enemy. The canon narrates the day as the national sin of the Patria Vieja; its expiation follows at once, for word arrives that Osorio is over the Cachapoal, and O'Higgins, swallowing the feud whole, puts himself and his men under Carrera's orders to face the invader.

stops.name: Rancagua, the first day of the siege
stops.campa: On the morning of 1 October 1814 Osorio's five thousand close the four streets of Rancagua upon O'Higgins and seventeen hundred men behind trenches of adobe and carts. Summoned to surrender, O'Higgins answers by hoisting a black flag over the tower of the plaza church: no quarter asked, none given. All day the assaults break against the trenches; the defenders' water is cut; the wounded are dragged into the church. On the hill to the north, Carrera's third division stands watching, and the promised relief does not come.

stops.name: Rancagua, the breakout through the flames
stops.campa: Thirty-three hours into the siege the town burns around the survivors, the cannon are out of grape, and the last water is gone. O'Higgins, twice wounded, mounts what horses remain and gives the order the nation still recites. Two hundred horsemen burst from the plaza through fire and bayonets, O'Higgins at the point, and cut their way clean through Osorio's army into the open valley. The Patria Vieja dies at Rancagua, but its seed escapes on horseback through the flames. The canon calls the breakout the baptism of fire of the Chilean nation.
stops.quote: ¡Los Dragones a caballo! ¡Monte a caballo todo el que pueda! ¡Nos abriremos paso en medio del enemigo!
stops.quote_source: Battle tradition of Rancagua, 2 October 1814 (Academia de Historia Militar de Chile; Barros Arana)

stops.name: The Uspallata pass, the emigration over the Andes
stops.campa: The remnant of a nation goes up into the cordillera: soldiers with bound wounds, friars, women with children on mules, among them doña Isabel and Rosa, the Liberator's mother and sister, riding with the baggage of defeat. O'Higgins, his wounds still open, shepherds the column through the October snows of the Uspallata route. Behind them Las Canteras is ash and the royalist terror begins; ahead is Mendoza and an unknown governor named San Martín. The canon frames the crossing as the nation's exodus: Chile carried over the mountains in saddlebags.

stops.name: Mendoza, the meeting with San Martín
stops.campa: The Governor-Intendant of Cuyo rides out to receive the defeated. José de San Martín and Bernardo O'Higgins clasp hands for the first time: two initiates of the same London lodge, meeting as if by countersign. San Martín, weighing the exiles, sides with O'Higgins against Carrera's pretensions, and around these two the great design takes shape: an army forged in Mendoza to retake Chile and carry the war by sea to Lima itself. The canon dates the continental strategy of liberation from this handclasp.

stops.name: El Plumerillo, forging the Army of the Andes
stops.campa: On the dusty camp ground of El Plumerillo north of Mendoza the Army of the Andes is hammered into being, and O'Higgins drills the Chilean units day after day: the escapees of Rancagua now sergeants, the huachos and inquilinos now grenadiers. Fray Luis Beltrán casts cannon in his forge like a warrior-monk; the women of Cuyo sew uniforms; San Martín spreads false maps for the Viceroy's spies. O'Higgins is given command of a division. Two years of exile are compressed into one instrument of war.

stops.name: Mendoza, the blessing of the flag and the Virgin made General
stops.campa: On 5 January 1817, before the army drawn up in the plaza of Mendoza, the new flag of the Andes is blessed and Our Lady of Carmen is proclaimed Patroness and Generala of the army; San Martín lays his baton in her hand. O'Higgins stands at the head of his division as the standard dips before the image. The campaign that follows is fought, the canon insists, under her mantle: every dispatch of victory will be laid at her feet, and O'Higgins will yet build her a temple on a battlefield not yet chosen.

stops.name: The Paso de los Patos, commanding a column across the roof of America
stops.campa: The army goes up by six passes at once, and O'Higgins leads a division of the main body over the Paso de los Patos: four thousand metres of wind and scree, mules dying by the hundred, cannon dismounted and dragged on sledges of hide. He rides the column front to rear in the thin air, the man of the hot Laja valleys now a commander in the ice. On the far side lies Chile. The canon sets the crossing beside Hannibal's and gives O'Higgins his place in it: not a passenger of the epic, but a driver of it.

stops.name: Las Coimas, valley of Putaendo, first blood in Chile
stops.campa: The vanguard comes down out of the rocks into the green of Putaendo, and at Las Coimas on 7 February the patriot horse scatters the royalist advance parties. The army of the exiles stands again on Chilean soil, two years and four months after the flames of Rancagua. Guasos come down from the hills with fruit and intelligence; the valley declares itself. O'Higgins presses the columns toward the cuesta of Chacabuco, where Marcó del Pont's army gathers to bar the road to Santiago.

stops.name: Chacabuco, the charge of 12 February 1817
stops.campa: The plan gives O'Higgins the eastern road and orders him to wait for Soler's flanking column. Before noon, seeing the royalists forming to escape the trap, O'Higgins waits no longer: he hurls his fifteen hundred straight at the line with the bayonet. The first charge is thrown back from the ravines; he re-forms and charges again as Soler's guns open on the flank, and the royalist army disintegrates. By dusk the road to Santiago is open and the Reconquista is dead. San Martín's plan won the campaign, says the canon, but the arrebato of O'Higgins won the day.

stops.name: Santiago, Supreme Director of Chile
stops.campa: Santiago pours into the streets to receive the victors. An open cabildo offers the supreme command to San Martín, who refuses it: his road runs to Lima. On 16 February 1817 the assembly acclaims Bernardo O'Higgins Supreme Director of Chile. The huacho of Chillán, denied his father's face, now bears the fatherhood of the nation itself. He takes the office as the lodge intended: not a throne but a lever, to finish the war in the south and build the fleet that will carry the revolution to Peru.

stops.name: Talcahuano, the assault on the last fortress
stops.campa: The war is not finished: the royalist remnant fortifies the peninsula of Talcahuano, and through the southern winter O'Higgins directs the siege in person, back on the ground of his first campaigns. On 6 December 1817 he launches the great night assault against the trenches; the columns carry the first works and break against the second, and the ditches fill with the bravest of the army. He raises the siege when word comes that Osorio has landed again from Peru with a new invasion. The canon keeps Talcahuano as the hard lesson before the crown of Maipú.
